answers.primary: A programmatic multi-step workflow (a dynamic workflow driven by the harness, entered through one slash command) that enumerates the route handler files, fans out one audit subagent per file with an identical prompt, then fans out one adversarial verifier subagent per candidate finding before anything is written to the report. The command plus the workflow definition live in the repo so the identical pass reruns next quarter by name.
answers.rejected_alternative: Ad hoc parallel subagent dispatch from the main conversation, rejected because the main model re-decides the batching, the prompt wording and the verification gate on every run, so a 400 file pass is neither uniform nor reproducible a quarter later.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: the workflow runner, not the model, decides that every enumerated file gets a pass and that no finding reaches the report without a verifier step. The model only supplies the judgement inside each step.
answers.context_boundary: Each file audit and each verification runs in its own subagent context window holding that file and its diff; only a structured finding record (or a rejection) crosses back. The orchestrating conversation never holds 400 file bodies, just the merged verified report.
answers.lifecycle: Fires when the single command is invoked, once a quarter; it stops when every enumerated file has been audited and every candidate finding adjudicated, and it has no standing effect on the session between runs.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on coverage: a stale or wrong file glob silently shrinks the population and the run still reports success, and false negatives are invisible because nothing verifies the absence of a finding. The adversarial verifier also biases toward suppression, so real authorization gaps can be argued away, and a 400 unit run can exhaust time or budget partway and leave a partial report that reads as complete.
answers.version_caveat: Parallel subagent fan-out and slash commands are long-standing and broadly available; the declarative workflow runner that makes the loop harness-owned is a newer capability and I cannot state its exact minimum version, feature flag or plan gate from memory, so the workflow form has to be validated against the installed build before this is relied on quarterly.

answers.primary: An agent team: five peer teammates launched together, each seeded with one hypothesis, using inter-agent messaging so they can read and attack each other's claims while the investigation is live, with a lead responsible for writing the surviving consensus to a findings document on disk.
answers.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents, rejected because subagent contexts are mutually invisible, so falsification could only happen after the fact by relaying reports through the parent, which is a review, not a debate.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model owns the outcome. The harness only routes messages and holds the separate context windows; nothing mechanical forces a teammate to genuinely attempt falsification or to concede when refuted.
answers.context_boundary: Each investigator has its own window holding its own logs, traces and reproduction attempts; what crosses between them is messages, and what crosses to my conversation is the lead's synthesis. The findings document on disk is the durable artifact that outlives all five contexts.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the team is launched with the five hypotheses and ends when consensus is written and the team is torn down; the teammates do not persist afterwards and their contexts are discarded.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. The likeliest failure is premature convergence: one plausible teammate anchors the others and the debate ratifies a wrong cause with the appearance of rigour. Cost is also roughly five concurrent contexts plus message traffic, and teammates can spend the budget arguing rather than reproducing the drop.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams with peer messaging are a recent addition and to my knowledge still carry experimental or opt-in status; I cannot state the exact version, setting name or plan tier that enables them, so this design should be confirmed against the installed build rather than assumed.

answers.primary: A subagent (a test-runner agent defined in the project's agents directory, with Bash allowed) that executes the suite inside its own context and returns only the failing test identifiers with their error messages, ideally invoked through a slash command so the shape is fixed.
answers.rejected_alternative: Running the suite in the main thread with the output piped through a filter or a PostToolUse hook that truncates Bash results, rejected because a byte-level filter cannot tell a failing assertion from noise, and one mistaken invocation still dumps the full log into my window.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness owns the boundary, because a subagent transcript is structurally separate and its tool results never enter the parent window, while the model owns fidelity, because it decides what counts as a failure worth reporting.
answers.context_boundary: The tens of thousands of lines live and die inside the subagent's context. Only the subagent's final message, the failure list, crosses into my conversation; the raw log does not, and does not survive the subagent.
answers.lifecycle: Runs on each explicit invocation of the runner and ends when the report is returned; it imposes nothing between invocations, and the isolated context is discarded with the run.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on completeness rather than on volume: the subagent can paraphrase, merge or drop failures and I have no way to notice, because the evidence it summarized is gone. If the suite fails in hundreds of tests, the summary itself can be large enough to flood the parent, and nothing prevents me from running the suite directly in the main thread unless a hook denies that command there.
answers.version_caveat: Subagents with per-agent tool allowlists and model selection are a stable, broadly available mechanism with no plan gate that I am aware of; I cannot state the exact release that introduced the frontmatter fields, so treat specific field names as needing verification against the installed version.

answers.primary: An agent team of three peers, one per layer (frontend, backend API, tests), communicating over the team's inter-agent messaging so an interface contract change announced by the backend worker reaches the other two while the work is still in flight, and addressable individually so I can redirect one worker without going through a coordinator.
answers.rejected_alternative: Three parallel subagents, rejected on both requirements: subagents cannot message each other as the contract evolves, and there is no way to attach to a running subagent to steer it, since the only interface is the prompt in and the report out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model owns the outcome. The harness provides separate windows, the message bus and the ability to direct input at one member; whether the contract actually stays consistent across three layers is a model judgement with no mechanical gate.
answers.context_boundary: Each worker holds only its own layer's files in its own window. Contract updates and questions cross as messages between workers, and my instructions cross into whichever worker I address; the shared source tree is the other, riskier, channel.
answers.lifecycle: Runs for the duration of the feature, from team launch until the three layers agree the work is done and the team is disbanded; nothing persists into later sessions except the code and any notes written to disk.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory. Two real failures: contract drift despite the messaging, because a worker can miss or ignore a message and there is no schema that mechanically binds the three layers, and write collisions, because peers editing a shared tree concurrently can clobber each other in files that straddle layers such as shared types. Cost is three concurrent contexts plus traffic.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams, peer messaging and direct addressing of an individual member are recent and, as far as I know, still opt-in or experimental; I cannot name the exact version, flag or plan requirement, so the direct-redirect capability in particular should be verified on the installed build before the plan depends on it.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow: a harness-driven loop whose body is run type check, apply fixes, re-run, with a termination predicate encoded in the workflow (green, or two consecutive rounds with no reduction in the error set). Each round's checker invocation is best delegated to a subagent so the compiler spew stays out of the loop's own context.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill or slash command that instructs the model to keep looping, rejected because the model re-evaluates the stopping condition every round in prose, which is exactly the babysitting and re-deciding that is meant to be removed; it stops early on a plausible-sounding excuse or loops past the no-progress point.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns iteration and termination. The model owns only the content of each round, which fixes to apply; it does not get a vote on whether another round happens.
answers.context_boundary: The loop and its counters live in the session or workflow state; if each check runs in a subagent, the raw type-checker output stays there and only the error list and the applied diff cross back, which is what keeps a ten-round loop from filling the window.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on one invocation and ends on the first satisfied predicate: a clean type check, or the second consecutive round with no progress. It applies to nothing outside that invocation.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open in the expensive direction. The progress metric is the weak point: error counts oscillate as fixes surface new errors, so a naive no-progress test either halts a healthy loop or never trips. Worse, the loop's own success test cannot distinguish a real fix from a suppression, so the model can reach green by widening types, adding any, or adding ignore directives, and the workflow will report success.
answers.version_caveat: The looping construct is the version-sensitive part: harness-driven workflow loops with predicates are newer than skills, hooks and subagents, and I cannot state the version, flag or plan tier that provides them. If the installed build lacks them, the fallback is an external script or the Agent SDK driving repeated headless invocations, which keeps the loop out of the model's hands.

answers.primary: A dynamic workflow that enumerates the roughly 500 component files and dispatches one migration subagent per file, each working in its own isolated checkout (a git worktree or equivalent copy) so no two edits touch the same tree, with a verification step (build or targeted test of that component) that must pass before the unit is marked done and merged back.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because 500 uniform transforms need no peer discussion at all; a team adds messaging cost and, worse, puts communicating peers into a shared tree, which is the precise collision the isolated copies exist to prevent.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: enumeration, per-unit isolation, dispatch and the verify-before-done gate are mechanical steps the runner performs. The model owns only the transform inside each unit.
answers.context_boundary: One subagent context per file, holding that file and its imports; what crosses back is a pass or fail plus a pointer to the branch or diff, not the file content. The orchestrator holds a ledger of 500 statuses, never 500 file bodies.
answers.lifecycle: One invocation over a fixed enumerated list; it ends when every unit is done or a failure budget trips, and it leaves behind branches or worktrees that must be reaped, which is state that outlives the run.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on integration. Per-file verification can pass 500 times while the aggregate is broken, because cross-file concerns (shared theme objects, global style resets, a design token file every component imports) are invisible to a single-file unit. Isolated copies also defer every conflict to merge time, and stragglers or silently skipped units are easy to miss in a ledger that large.
answers.version_caveat: Isolated-copy execution depends on git worktrees being usable in the repo, which is a repository property rather than a Claude Code version gate. The workflow runner that drives the fan-out and the verify gate is the newer piece and I cannot state its exact version, flag or plan requirement; without it the same shape is achievable with batched subagent dispatch driven by a script or the Agent SDK.

answers.primary: Parallel subagent fan-out with an explicit merge step: one reviewer subagent per changed file, dispatched in batches, each returning a structured finding list, followed by a single reduce pass (main thread or a dedicated merge subagent) that deduplicates and ranks. Fixed behind a slash command so the same PR review shape repeats.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because the scenario explicitly has nothing for the reviewers to say to each other; peer messaging would add per-message cost and coordination latency to what is a pure map-reduce.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model owns the outcome: it decides the dispatch, the batching and above all the merge, which is where judgement about duplicates and severity lives. The harness only guarantees that the 60 reviewer contexts stay separate.
answers.context_boundary: Each reviewer sees one file's diff plus whatever it opens, in its own window. Only finding lists cross back. The main window ends up holding 60 finding lists, which is where the context does refill, so the merge step is the real bottleneck, not the fan-out.
answers.lifecycle: Runs per pull request on invocation and ends when the single ranked summary is produced; it leaves no standing rule, and the reviewer contexts are discarded.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open, in a way that is specific to one-file-per-reviewer: any defect that only exists across files (a caller updated but not its callee, a renamed field, a changed invariant) is structurally invisible because no reviewer ever sees both sides. Secondarily, the same issue reported by ten reviewers relies entirely on the merge pass to collapse, and a weak merge produces an inflated, misranked summary.
answers.version_caveat: Subagents and parallel dispatch are stable and broadly available. There is a concurrency cap on simultaneously running subagents whose exact number I cannot state from memory, so 60 units will be executed in waves rather than all at once, and any plan that assumes true 60-way parallelism should check the installed limit.

answers.primary: A sequenced pipeline of three subagents (profiler, fixer, verifier) driven by one orchestration entry point, a slash command or a workflow, where each stage receives the previous stage's structured output as its input contract: the profiler emits an issue list, the fixer is scoped to that list, the verifier re-measures against it.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent team, rejected because peer concurrency is actively harmful here: strict ordering is the requirement, and three communicating peers writing the same handful of hot files would clobber each other's edits with no ordering guarantee.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns ordering if the sequence is expressed as a workflow or a command with fixed steps; the model owns the content of each stage, and critically the model owns whether the fixer actually stays inside the issue list, which nothing enforces.
answers.context_boundary: Three separate context windows, one per stage. What crosses is the handoff artifact only: the issue list, then the change list with measurements. The orchestrating conversation keeps the handoffs, not the profiles or the file bodies, so the parent stays small even though all three stages read the same hot files.
answers.lifecycle: One invocation, three phases in order, ending when the verifier reports; each stage's context is discarded at its own boundary, so nothing carries forward except the written handoff and the edits on disk.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on scope and on independence. The fixer can drift beyond exactly what was found, because the issue list is a prompt, not a constraint, and edits to hot files may fix a measured problem while regressing an unmeasured one. The verifier is only meaningful if it re-measures rather than reading the fixer's own claims; if it does the latter, the pipeline self-certifies and the failure is silent.
answers.version_caveat: This is expressible today with plain sequential subagent invocations, which are stable and ungated, so nothing here strictly requires a new feature. Only the declarative form, where the runner rather than the model guarantees the order, depends on the newer workflow capability whose version, flag and plan requirements I cannot state from memory.

answers.primary: An agent team of three explorers (user experience, technical architecture, devil's advocate) launched as peers with inter-agent messaging so each can react to arguments as the others form them, and individually addressable so I can attach to one mid-flight and redirect it.
answers.rejected_alternative: Three parallel subagents, rejected because isolated contexts can only be compared after all three finish, which produces three parallel monologues plus a post-hoc merge, not perspectives reacting to each other, and offers no way to steer one while it runs.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model owns the outcome. The harness only supplies the separate windows, the message routing and the ability to direct my input at one member; the quality of the exploration, and whether the devil's advocate actually bites, is entirely model behaviour.
answers.context_boundary: Each explorer reasons in its own window with its own accumulating argument. Arguments cross between them as messages, and my redirection crosses into one of them; my conversation sees the synthesis unless I attach, and nothing is durable unless a design document is explicitly written to disk.
answers.lifecycle: Runs from team launch until a design direction is chosen and the team is stopped. Because it is pre-commitment exploration it stops applying the moment the design is settled, and it leaves no artifact behind by default.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory throughout. The characteristic failure is convergence theatre: with live messaging the two constructive explorers anchor on one design and the devil's advocate either capitulates or degenerates into generic objections, and the transcript reads as having stress-tested a design it merely rehearsed. Cost is three concurrent contexts plus a debate that has no natural stopping point.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams and mid-flight addressing of a single member are recent and, to my knowledge, opt-in or experimental; I cannot state the version, setting or plan tier that enables them. If the installed build lacks live addressing, the fallback is sequential rounds of subagents with a human-relayed critique, which loses the reacting-as-they-form property.

answers.primary: One orchestrator subagent that performs the review pass and, inside its own context, dispatches one independent verifier subagent per finding, returning exactly one merged verified summary. Nesting the whole thing under a single top-level delegation is what keeps every intermediate exchange below the boundary of my conversation.
answers.rejected_alternative: Dispatching the per-finding verifiers from the main thread, rejected because each verifier's report would then land in my window; the fan-out would be correct but the confidentiality requirement, that no per-finding chatter reaches me, would be violated by construction.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness owns the context boundary, since a nested delegation's transcript is structurally inaccessible to the parent, while the model owns the substance, that each finding really was handed to a fresh verifier rather than re-checked inline.
answers.context_boundary: Two levels of isolation. Each verifier holds one finding and the evidence it gathers; the orchestrator holds the review plus 5 to 10 verdicts; only the orchestrator's single final message crosses into my conversation. Everything below that line is discarded when the run ends.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on invocation of the review command over the recent change set and ends when the one summary is returned; the nested contexts are torn down with it and nothing persists into the session.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and, worse, fails invisibly. If nested dispatch is unavailable or the orchestrator simply declines to use it, the orchestrator verifies its own findings inline, which is self-review; the returned summary looks identical either way and I cannot tell from my side because the intermediate layer is exactly what I asked not to see. A rubber-stamping verifier produces the same undetectable result.
answers.version_caveat: Whether a subagent may itself spawn subagents is the load-bearing uncertainty here: that capability has been restricted in some versions of Claude Code and I cannot state from memory which version permits it or what flag enables it. Verify nested dispatch on the installed build; if it is not permitted, restructure as a workflow whose intermediate steps are not surfaced, or accept the chatter and post-filter.
